idiom_name: const-qualified borrows + whole-struct copies (const is shallow, no immutable aggregates)
implementation_notes: C has no immutable objects: const makes an lvalue non-modifiable, so a const struct pointer cannot be written through, and passing or returning a struct by value hands the caller its own copy - those two conventions are what replace an immutable type with copy-with methods. The discipline has to be hand-built everywhere: keep the type definition in a header but its fields behind accessor functions, return copies (a foo_copy function, buffer copies) instead of pointers into internal storage, and qualify every read path const. Because const is shallow - a const struct pointer still allows writes through pointers stored inside the struct unless each level is qualified - and because a const object may live in read-only memory, casting the qualifier away and writing is undefined behaviour, not a shortcut. The classic immutable-type structure is still worth building when one opaque handle wraps a larger buffer whose copies would be expensive: allocate a new handle, copy, and return it.
pitfalls: const is not deep: a const struct pointer protects the members only through that lvalue, and pointers stored in the struct can still be used to modify the pointees unless each level is const-qualified.
Casting away const and writing is undefined behaviour; const objects may be placed in read-only memory, so the write faults instead of silently working.
Returning a pointer to an internal static or const buffer to avoid a copy makes the caller's next call silently overwrite data it still holds.
